arXiv:2505.16822v2 [math.NT] 11 Nov 2025

Quantitative bounds in a popular polynomial Szemerédi theorem

Xuancheng Shao Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, 40506, USA Email address: xuancheng.shao@uky.edu and Mengdi Wang Address: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Lausanne, Switzerland Email address: mengdi.wang@epfl.ch
Abstract.

We obtain polylogarithmic bounds in the polynomial Szemerédi theorem when the polynomials have distinct degrees and zero constant terms. Specifically, let P1,…,Pm∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[y] be polynomials with distinct degrees, each having zero constant term. Then there exists a constant c=c⁡(P1,…,Pm)>0c=c(P_{1},\dots,P_{m})>0 such that any subset A⊂{1,2,…,N}A\subset\{1,2,\dots,N\} of density at least (log⁡N)−c(\log N)^{-c} contains a nontrivial polynomial progression of the form x,x+P1​(y),…,x+Pm​(y)x,x+P_{1}(y),\dots,x+P_{m}(y). In addition, we prove an effective “popular” version, showing that every dense subset AA has some non-zero yy such that the number of polynomial progressions in AA with this difference yy is asymptotically at least as large as in a random set of the same density as AA.

1. Introduction

The quest to understand the ubiquity of arithmetic structures within subsets of integers has driven some of the most profound advances in additive combinatorics. Szemerédi’s landmark theorem states that every subset of the integers with positive density contains non-trivial kk-term arithmetic progressions (kk-APs) for every natural number kk. A pivotal contribution came from Gowers [11], who introduced uniformity norms to furnish a quantitative bound for Szemerédi’s theorem, establishing that any subset of {1,2,…,N}\{1,2,\dots,N\} which does not contain non-trivial kk-APs must have density O⁡((log⁡log⁡N)−ck)O((\log\log N)^{-c_{k}}) for some constant ck>0c_{k}>0. Over the years, the pursuit of quantitative bounds in Szemerédi’s theorem has remained extremely active, leading to many significant developments. For example, Kelley and Meka [19] established a bound of the shape O⁡(exp⁡(−c​(log⁡N)1/12))O(\exp(-c(\log N)^{1/12})) for the case k=3k=3, where the exponent 1/121/12 is later improved to 1/91/9 by Bloom and Sisask [3]. Green and Tao [17] achieved a polylogarithmic bound for k=4k=4. Leng, Sah, and Sawhney [20] improved Gowers’ bound to O⁡(exp⁡(−(log⁡log⁡N)ck))O(\exp(-(\log\log N)^{c_{k}})) for general k⩾5k\geqslant 5.

The scope of such results broadened significantly with the polynomial Szemerédi theorem of Bergelson and Leibman [2], which established that every subset of the integers with positive density contains polynomial progressions of the form x,x+P1​(y),…,x+Pm​(y)x,x+P_{1}(y),\dots,x+P_{m}(y) with y≠0y\neq 0, where P1,…,Pm∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[y] and each has zero constant term. Their proof was rooted in ergodic theory and was thus non-quantitative.

The density increment method has long served as the primary tool for deriving quantitative bounds for general additive patterns. However, applying this strategy to more complex polynomial configurations introduces additional difficulties; see [29, Section 2.2] for a detailed discussion. While a quantitative version of the general polynomial Szemerédi theorem remains an open challenge, progress has been made in certain special cases. We summarize some of these developments below and refer the reader to [25] for for a more in-depth overview of the history of quantitative results in the polynomial Szemerédi theorem both in the integers and in the finite field setting.

  • •

    For Sarközy’s theorem on square differences (i.e. x,x+y2x,x+y^{2}), Green and Sawhney [14] achieved quantitative bounds of the form O⁡(exp⁡(−c​log⁡N))O(\exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})).

  • •

    When P1,⋯,PmP_{1},\cdots,P_{m} are homogeneous and have the same degree, Prendiville [29] achieved bounds of the form O⁡((log⁡log⁡N)−c)O((\log\log N)^{-c}) (which can likely be improved to O⁡(exp⁡(−(log⁡log⁡N)c))O(\exp(-(\log\log N)^{c})) using the quasipolynomial bounds in the inverse theorem for the Gowers norms from [21], together with the density increment strategy of Heath-Brown and Szemerédi).

  • •

    For the nonlinear Roth configuration (i.e. x,x+y,x+y2x,x+y,x+y^{2}), Peluse and Prendiville [27, 26] achieved quantitative bounds of the form O⁡((log⁡N)−c)O((\log N)^{-c}).

  • •

    Peluse [25] extended these techniques from the nonlinear Roth configuration to more general polynomial progressions when P1,…,PmP_{1},\dots,P_{m} have distinct degrees and each has zero constant term. She obtained bounds of the form O⁡((log⁡log⁡N)−c)O((\log\log N)^{-c}) for subsets of {1,2,…,N}\{1,2,\dots,N\} that do not contain such configurations.

The first main result of this paper is an improvement of the quantitative bound in Peluse’s result [25, Theorem 1.1].

Theorem 1.1 (Density bound).

Let P1,…,Pm∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[y] be polynomials with distinct degrees, each having zero constant term. If A⊂{1,2,…,N}A\subset\{1,2,\dots,N\} does not contain a polynomial progression of the form

x,x+P1​(y),…,x+Pm​(y)with ​y≠0,x,x+P_{1}(y),\dots,x+P_{m}(y)\ \ \text{with }y\neq 0,

then

|A|≪N(log⁡N)c|A|\ll\frac{N}{(\log N)^{c}}

for some constant c>0c>0 depending only on P1,…,PmP_{1},\dots,P_{m}.

In the “structure vs. randomness” framework underlying the density increment argument, if a set AA is not pseudorandom, then the number of additive configurations in this set AA may deviate significantly from the random bound. Bergelson, Host, and Kra [1] posed the question of whether there always exists a nonzero difference yy for which the number of configurations in AA with difference parameter yy is at least as large as the random bound. For example, in the case when the configurations are 33-APs, the question asks for A⊂{1,2,⋯,N}A\subset\{1,2,\cdots,N\} with |A|=δ​N|A|=\delta N, whether there exists y≠0y\neq 0 such that

#{x∈A:x,x+y,x+2y∈A}⩾(δ3−o(1))N.\#\{x\in A:x,x+y,x+2y\in A\}\geqslant(\delta^{3}-o(1))N.

Such yy is loosely referred as a “popular difference”. This topic in the ergodic setting was initially explored by Bergelson, Host, and Kra [1] and also studied in [9, 10, 4]. We list some notable results below in the arithmetic setting, and refer the readers to [28] for more contexts surrounding the popular difference results.

  • •

    The existence of popular differences is proved by Green [13] for 33-APs and by Green and Tao [16] for 44-APs. When k⩾5k\geqslant 5, a counterexample was built by Ruzsa in the appendix to [1].

  • •

    The quantitative aspects of popular common differences in 3-APs were studied in [7, 6, 5].

  • •

    Linear configurations were classified in [30] according to when popular differences are guaranteed to exist.

  • •

    Popular differences for corners (x1,x2),(x1+y,x2),(x1,x2+y)(x_{1},x_{2}),(x_{1}+y,x_{2}),(x_{1},x_{2}+y) are studied in [23, 8].

  • •

    The existence of popular differences for special polynomial progressions is proved by Lyall and Magyar [22] for the square differences x,x+y2x,x+y^{2} and by Peluse, Prendiville, and the first author [28] for the nonlinear Roth pattern x,x+y,x+y2x,x+y,x+y^{2}.

In this paper, we prove, with effective bounds, the existence of popular differences in general polynomial progressions when the polynomials have distinct degrees and each has zero constant term.

Theorem 1.2 (Popular difference).

Let P1,…,Pm∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[y] be polynomials with distinct degrees, each having zero constant term. Let A⊂{1,2,…,N}A\subset\{1,2,\dots,N\} be a subset with |A|⩾δ​N|A|\geqslant\delta N and let ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2). Then either N⩽exp⁡(exp⁡(ε−OP1,…,Pm​(1)))N\leqslant\exp(\exp(\varepsilon^{-O_{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}}(1)})) or there exists a positive integer yy such that

#⁡{x∈A:x+Pi​(y)∈A​ for each ​1⩽i⩽m}⩾(δm+1−ε)​N.\#\{x\in A:x+P_{i}(y)\in A\text{ for each }1\leqslant i\leqslant m\}\geqslant(\delta^{m+1}-\varepsilon)N.

The proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 are based on an inverse theorem. As the final part of the introduction, we present a simplified version of our more general result, Theorem 2.4. Suppose that N,M⩾1N,M\geqslant 1, P1,…,Pm∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[y] are polynomials and f0,…,fm:ℤ→ℂf_{0},\dots,f_{m}:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} are functions supported on the interval [N][N]. We define the associated counting operator as follows:

(1.1) ΛP1,…,PmN,M(f0,…,fm):=1N​M∑x∈ℤ∑y∈[M]f0(x)f1(x+P1(y))⋯fm(x+Pm(y)).\displaystyle\Lambda_{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}}^{N,M}(f_{0},\dots,f_{m}):=\frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{y\in[M]}f_{0}(x)f_{1}(x+P_{1}(y))\cdots f_{m}(x+P_{m}(y)).
Theorem 1.3 (Inverse theorem).

Let P1,…,Pm∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[y] be polynomials with distinct degrees, and let their coefficients be bounded by CC. Let d=m​a​x1⩽i⩽m​deg⁡Pid=max_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}\deg P_{i}. Let N,MN,M be positive integers with M≍CN1/dM\asymp_{C}N^{1/d}, and let δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2). Suppose that f0,…,fm:ℤ→ℂf_{0},\dots,f_{m}:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} are 11-bounded functions supported on [N][N]. If

|ΛP1,…,PmN,M​(f0,…,fm)|⩾δ.\bigl|\Lambda_{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}}^{N,M}(f_{0},\dots,f_{m})\bigr|\geqslant\delta.

Then either M≪C,dδ−Od​(1)M\ll_{C,d}\delta^{-O_{d}(1)} or there exists a positive integer q≪C,dδ−Od​(1)q\ll_{C,d}\delta^{-O_{d}(1)} and a 11-bounded function ϕi:ℤ→ℂ\phi_{i}:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} for each 1⩽i⩽m1\leqslant i\leqslant m which is OC,d​(δ−Od​(1)​M−deg⁡Pi)O_{C,d}(\delta^{-O_{d}(1)}M^{-\deg P_{i}})-Lipschitz along q⋅ℤq\cdot\mathbb{Z}, such that

|∑x∈ℤfi(x)ϕi(x)|≫C,dδOd​(1)N.\bigl|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{i}(x)\phi_{i}(x)\bigr|\gg_{C,d}\delta^{O_{d}(1)}N.

The definition of CC-Lipschitz function is given in Definition 2.1. For intuition, we encourage the reader to think of ϕi\phi_{i} as a phase function of the form x↦e⁡(αi​x)x\mapsto e(\alpha_{i}x) with ‖qαi‖≪C,dδ−Od​(1)M−deg⁡Pi\left\|q\alpha_{i}\right\|\ll_{C,d}\delta^{-O_{d}(1)}M^{-\deg P_{i}}. Alternatively, ϕi\phi_{i} is almost constant on progressions of length Θ⁡(δOd​(1)​Mdeg⁡Pi)\Theta(\delta^{O_{d}(1)}M^{\deg P_{i}}) and common difference qq. Even though qq is independent of ii, this is unimportant since one could simply take qq to be the least common multiple of all qiq_{i}’s if qq is allowed to depend on ii, while maintaining the upper bound for qq.

Compared to Peluse’s inverse theorem [25, Theorem 3.3] which concludes correlation only for the fif_{i} corresponding to the lowest degree polynomial, our inverse theorem gives such conclusions for every fif_{i}. This generalization, which is fundamental in getting the polylogarithmic bound in Theorem 1.1 and also in obtaining the popular difference result, is largely based on arguments of Peluse [25] incorporated with some technical generalizations. Instead of proving Theorem 1.3 directly, we will in fact prove a slightly more general version of it, Theorem 2.4. See the discussions following the statement of Theorem 2.4 for a brief overview of the proof ideas.

We would like to make some remarks on general polynomial sequences. When the leading coefficients of the highest-degree terms among P1,…,PmP_{1},\dots,P_{m} are distinct, the sequence can be controlled by a Gowers UsU^{s}-norm for some s>2s>2. In other cases, it can only be controlled by an average of box norms. Ideally, in such situations, some suitable local inverse theorems can be applied. As suggested by Leng–Sah–Sawhney [20], one can obtain quantitative density bounds for linear forms, since the inverse theorem implies that ff correlates with a periodic function ϕ\phi. However, the period of ϕ\phi is typically of order N1−ηN^{1-\eta} for some small η>0\eta>0, which means that the density increment achieved at each step is not sufficiently effective. This is also the reason why the density increment argument fails for general polynomial sequences.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we prove our main inverse theorem, Theorem 2.4 (of which Theorem 1.3 is a special case). In Section 3 we develop the theory of local factors which are necessary for our weak regularity lemmas. In Section 4 we prove Theorem 1.1 by establishing a regularity lemma and using the density increment argument, generalizing Peluse and Prendiville’s work [26] on the nonlinear Roth pattern. In Section 5 we prove Theorem 1.2 by establishing a second weak regularity lemma.

2. Inverse theorems

The goal of this section is to prove the inverse theorem which is the key to both Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. It asserts that if the counting expression (1.1) is large, then the functions exhibit correlation with certain Lipschitz functions. We adopt the same definition as [26, Definition 6.1].

Definition 2.1 (CC-Lipschitz).

A function ϕ:ℤ→ℂ\phi:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} is said to be CC–Lipschitz along q⋅ℤq\cdot\mathbb{Z} if for all x,y∈ℤx,y\in\mathbb{Z} we have

|ϕ⁡(x+q​y)−ϕ⁡(x)|⩽C​|y|.|\phi(x+qy)-\phi(x)|\leqslant C|y|.

Note that if α∈𝕋\alpha\in\mathbb{T} is a frequency such that ‖q​α‖\left\|q\alpha\right\| is sufficiently small for some positive integer q⩾1q\geqslant 1, then the linear phase function e(⋅α)e(\cdot\alpha) is (2​π​‖q​α‖)(2\pi\left\|q\alpha\right\|)-Lipschitz along q⋅ℤq\cdot\mathbb{Z}. Thus Lipschitz functions serve as an analogue to linear phase functions. The following lemma provides another class of Lipschitz functions.

Lemma 2.2.

Let q,Hq,H be positive integers and let f:ℤ→ℂf:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} be a 1-bounded function. Then the function

ϕ⁡(x)=𝔼h1,h2∈[H]​f​(x+q⁡(h1−h2))\phi(x)=\mathbb{E}_{h_{1},h_{2}\in[H]}f(x+q(h_{1}-h_{2}))

is O⁡(H−1)O(H^{-1})-Lipschitz along q⋅ℤq\cdot\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

[26, Lemma 6.2]. ∎

Before stating our general inverse theorems, we recall the notation of (C,q)(C,q)-coefficients from [25, Definition 3.1], which serves as an important index for tracking iteration steps.

Definition 2.3.

We say a polynomial P⁡(y)=ad​yd+⋯+a1​y∈ℤ⁡[y]P(y)=a_{d}y^{d}+\cdots+a_{1}y\in\mathbb{Z}[y] has (C,q)(C,q)-coefficients if |ai|⩽C​|ad||a_{i}|\leqslant C|a_{d}| for all 1⩽i⩽d−11\leqslant i\leqslant d-1 and ad=ad′​qd−1a_{d}=a_{d}^{\prime}q^{d-1} for some ad′∈ℤa_{d}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z} with 0<|ad′|⩽C0<|a_{d}^{\prime}|\leqslant C.

We are now ready to state the inverse theorem, of which Theorem 1.3 from the introduction is a special case corresponding to the situation where the polynomials have (C,1)(C,1)-coefficients and MM is relatively large. Recall the counting operator defined in (1.1).

Theorem 2.4 (Inverse theorem).

Let P1,…,Pm∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[y] be polynomials with (C,q)(C,q)-coefficients, and assume they have distinct degrees. Let d=m​a​x1⩽i⩽m​deg⁡Pid=max_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}\deg P_{i}. Let N,MN,M be positive integers with M⩽(N/qd−1)1/dM\leqslant(N/q^{d-1})^{1/d}, and let δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2). Suppose that f0,…,fm:ℤ→ℂf_{0},\dots,f_{m}:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} are 11-bounded functions supported on [N][N]. Let

|ΛP1,…,PmN,M​(f0,…,fm)|⩾δ.\bigl|\Lambda_{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}}^{N,M}(f_{0},\dots,f_{m})\bigr|\geqslant\delta.

Then either M≪C,d(q/δ)Od​(1)M\ll_{C,d}(q/\delta)^{O_{d}(1)}, or there exist positive integers q′≪C,dδ−Od​(1)q^{\prime}\ll_{C,d}\delta^{-O_{d}(1)} and b=Od​(1)b=O_{d}(1), as well as a 11-bounded function ϕi:ℤ→ℂ\phi_{i}:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} for each 1⩽i⩽m1\leqslant i\leqslant m which is OC,d​((q/δ)Od​(1)​M−deg⁡Pi)O_{C,d}((q/\delta)^{O_{d}(1)}M^{-\deg P_{i}})-Lipschitz along q′​qb⋅ℤq^{\prime}q^{b}\cdot\mathbb{Z}, such that

Assuming deg⁡P1=min1⩽i⩽m⁡deg⁡Pi\deg P_{1}=\min_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}\deg P_{i} without loss of generality, we note that Peluse’s inverse theorem [25, Theorem 3.3] implies the correlation result only for the function f1f_{1} in Theorem 2.4, under the assumption that M=(N/qd−1)1/dM=(N/q^{d-1})^{1/d} (or, slightly more generally, M≍C(N/qd−1)1/dM\asymp_{C}(N/q^{d-1})^{1/d}). Loosely speaking, if f1,…,fj−1f_{1},\dots,f_{j-1} correlates with Lipschitz functions ϕ1,…,ϕj−1\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{j-1}, respectively, then we will deduce that

from which we will then deduce that fjf_{j} also correlates with a Lipschitz function. This idea was discussed in [26, Section 7], and our implementation of it involves technical generalizations of Peluse’s arguments [25].

2.1. Inductive step

The proof of Proposition 2.5 adapts the proof of [25, Theorem 3.3] in [25, Section 9]. We outline the arguments before presenting the details. For N,M⩾1N,M\geqslant 1, polynomials P1,⋯,Pm∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1},\cdots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[y], functions f0,⋯,fℓ:ℤ→ℂf_{0},\cdots,f_{\ell}:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} supported on [N][N] and characters ψℓ+1,⋯,ψm:ℤ→ℂ\psi_{\ell+1},\cdots,\psi_{m}:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} of the form ψi​(x)=e⁡(αi​x)\psi_{i}(x)=e(\alpha_{i}x) with αi∈ℝ\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{R}, we define the counting operator

ΛP1,⋯,PmN,M​(f0,⋯,fℓ,ψℓ+1,⋯,ψm):=1N​M∑x∈ℤ∑y∈[M]f0(x)f1(x+P1(y))⋯fℓ(x+Pℓ(y))ψℓ+1(Pℓ+1(y))⋯ψm(Pm(y)).\begin{split}&\Lambda_{P_{1},\cdots,P_{m}}^{N,M}(f_{0},\cdots,f_{\ell};\psi_{\ell+1},\cdots,\psi_{m})\\ &:=\frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{y\in[M]}f_{0}(x)f_{1}(x+P_{1}(y))\cdots f_{\ell}(x+P_{\ell}(y))\psi_{\ell+1}(P_{\ell+1}(y))\cdots\psi_{m}(P_{m}(y)).\end{split}

When ℓ=m\ell=m this notation becomes (1.1). The first step in the proof of Proposition 2.5 involves repeated applications of the following lemma which is [25, Lemma 3.11].

Remark.

In the above argument, we used Lemma 2.8 based on the Hahn-Banach theorem to deduce intermediate conclusions for the dual functions GjG_{j}, which we then use to deduce conclusions for fj+1f_{j+1}. A modern way of executing this maneuver (in a much more sophisticated setting) was recently introduced by Manners [24] and referred to as “stashing”.

3. Local factors

In this section, we adopt the notation for factors from [15], originally derived from ergodic theory; see also [26, Section 4].

Definition 3.1 (Factor).

We define a factor ℬ\mathcal{B} of [N][N] to be a partition of [N][N], so that [N]=⊔B∈ℬB[N]=\sqcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}}B. A factor ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime} refines ℬ\mathcal{B} if every element of ℬ\mathcal{B} is a union of elements of ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}. The join ℬ1∨⋯∨ℬd\mathcal{B}_{1}\vee\dots\vee\mathcal{B}_{d} of factors ℬ1,…,ℬd\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{d} is the factor formed by taking the dd-fold intersections of the elements of ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}, …, ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d}, that is,

ℬ1∨⋯∨ℬd:={B1∩⋯∩Bd:Bi∈ℬi for i=1,…,d}.\mathcal{B}_{1}\vee\dots\vee\mathcal{B}_{d}:=\{B_{1}\cap\dots\cap B_{d}:B_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{i}\text{ for }i=1,\dots,d\}.
Definition 3.2 (Measurability, projection).

Given a factor ℬ\mathcal{B} of [N][N], we say that a function f:[N]→ℂf:[N]\to\mathbb{C} is ℬ\mathcal{B}-measurable if it is constant on the elements of ℬ\mathcal{B}. Define the projection of any function f:[N]→ℂf:[N]\to\mathbb{C} onto ℬ\mathcal{B} by

(3.1) Πℬ​f​(x)=𝔼y∈B⁡(x)​f​(y),\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}f(x)=\mathbb{E}_{y\in B(x)}f(y),

where B⁡(x)B(x) is the unique atom of ℬ\mathcal{B} containing xx.

Notice that Πℬ​f\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}f is ℬ\mathcal{B}-measurable and corresponds to the conditional expectation of ℬ\mathcal{B} with respect to the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the elements of ℬ\mathcal{B}. The following lemma illustrates why we work with projections onto factors: the l2l^{2}-norm of such projections is non-decreasing under refinement of the factor. For this reason, we refer to ‖Πℬ​f‖22\left\|\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}f\right\|_{2}^{2} as the energy.

Lemma 3.3 (Pythagoras theorem for projections).

Let ℬ,ℬ′\mathcal{B},\mathcal{B}^{\prime} be factors of [N][N] such that ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime} refines ℬ\mathcal{B}. Let f:[N]→ℂf:[N]\rightarrow\mathbb{C} be a function. Then

‖Πℬ′​f‖22=‖Πℬ​f‖22+‖Πℬ′​f−Πℬ​f‖22.\big\|\Pi_{\mathcal{B}^{\prime}}f\big\|_{2}^{2}=\big\|\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}f\big\|_{2}^{2}+\big\|\Pi_{\mathcal{B}^{\prime}}f-\Pi_{\mathcal{B}}f\big\|_{2}^{2}.
Proof.

See [26, Lemma 4.3]. ∎

In this paper we will exclusively work with factors whose atoms are arithmetic progressions.

Definition 3.4 (Local factor).

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a factor of [N][N]. Let q,M⩾1q,M\geqslant 1. We say that ℬ\mathcal{B} is a local factor of resolution MM and modulus qq if every atom of ℬ\mathcal{B} is an arithmetic progression of step qq and length in [M,2​M][M,2M].

For example, the trivial factor consisting of only one atom is a local factor of resolution NN and modulus 11. Our definition of local factors is motivated by, but slightly different from, the definition in [26], where the atoms are required to have length exactly MM. This flexibility leads to the following simple lemma which turns out to be rather convenient for our arguments.

Lemma 3.5 (Existence of local factors).

Let ℬ,ℬ′′\mathcal{B},\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime} be local factors of [N][N] of modulus qq and resolution M,M′′M,M^{\prime\prime}, respectively, and 100​M′′⩽M100M^{\prime\prime}\leqslant M. Suppose that ℬ′′\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime} refines ℬ\mathcal{B}. Then for any integer M′∈[10​M′′,M/10]M^{\prime}\in[10M^{\prime\prime},M/10], there exists a local factor ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime} of [N][N] of resolution M′M^{\prime} and modulus qq, such that ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime} refines ℬ\mathcal{B} and ℬ′′\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime} refines ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}.

Let PP be an arbitrary atom of ℬ\mathcal{B}, so that PP is an arithmetic progression of step qq and length in [M,2​M][M,2M]. Since ℬ′′\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime} refines ℬ\mathcal{B}, we have a partition

P=P1⊔P2⊔⋯⊔Pr,P=P_{1}\sqcup P_{2}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup P_{r},

where each PiP_{i} is an atom of ℬ′′\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime} which is an arithmetic progression of step qq and length in [M′′,2​M′′][M^{\prime\prime},2M^{\prime\prime}]. Without loss of generality, we may assume that all elements of PiP_{i} are smaller than all elements of PjP_{j} whenever i<ji<j. Let xi=|Pi|/M′x_{i}=|P_{i}|/M^{\prime} so that xi⩽[y,2​y]x_{i}\leqslant[y,2y] where y=M′′/M′⩽1/10y=M^{\prime\prime}/M^{\prime}\leqslant 1/10. Then

0=i0<i1<⋯<ik−1<ik=r,0=i_{0}<i_{1}<\cdots<i_{k-1}<i_{k}=r,

such that

xij−1+1+⋯+xij∈[1,2]x_{i_{j-1}+1}+\cdots+x_{i_{j}}\in[1,2]

Performing this procedure for each atom of ℬ\mathcal{B}, we obtain the desired refinement ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime} of ℬ\mathcal{B}.

To construct the sequence {ij}\{i_{j}\}, first choose a positive integer kk such that s/k∈[1.4,1.6]s/k\in[1.4,1.6]. The existence of such kk easily follows from s⩾10s\geqslant 10. Now, for each 1⩽j⩽k1\leqslant j\leqslant k, define iji_{j} to be the smallest index with the property that

In our proof of the popular difference result (Theorem 1.2), we need to work with a chain of local factors where each factor in the chain refines the next one.

Definition 3.6 (Local factor chain).

Let q,M1,…,Mmq,M_{1},\dots,M_{m} be positive integers. Let ℬ1,…,ℬm\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m} be local factors of [N][N] of modulus qq and resolution M1,…,MmM_{1},\dots,M_{m}, respectively. We say that (ℬ1,…,ℬm)(\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}) is a local factor chain of resolution (M1,…,Mm)(M_{1},\dots,M_{m}) and modulus qq, if ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} is a refinement of ℬi+1\mathcal{B}_{i+1} for each 1⩽i<m1\leqslant i<m.

Let (ℬ1,…,ℬm)(\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}) and (ℬ1′,…,ℬm′)(\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\prime},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\prime}) be two local factor chains. We say that (ℬ1′,…,ℬm′)(\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\prime},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\prime}) refines (ℬ1,…,ℬm)(\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}) if ℬi′\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\prime} refines ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} for each 1⩽i⩽m1\leqslant i\leqslant m.

To visualize the relationships between factors, we use the notation ℬ⟶ℬ′\mathcal{B}\longrightarrow\mathcal{B}^{\prime} to indicate that ℬ\mathcal{B} refines ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}. Thus a local factor chain (ℬ1,⋯,ℬm)(\mathcal{B}_{1},\cdots,\mathcal{B}_{m}) can be visualized as:

and the relationship that (ℬ1′,⋯,ℬm′)(\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\prime}) refines (ℬ1,⋯,ℬm)(\mathcal{B}_{1},\cdots,\mathcal{B}_{m}) can be visualized as:
Lemma 3.7 (Existence of local factor chains).

Let (ℬ1,…,ℬm)(\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}) be a local factor chain of [N][N] of resolution (M1,…,Mm)(M_{1},\dots,M_{m}) and modulus qq. Let q′,M1′,…,Mm′q^{\prime},M_{1}^{\prime},\dots,M_{m}^{\prime} be positive integers such that q′q^{\prime} is divisible by qq, and

10​Mi−1⩽q′q​Mi′⩽Mi1010M_{i-1}\leqslant\frac{q^{\prime}}{q}M_{i}^{\prime}\leqslant\frac{M_{i}}{10}

for each 1⩽i⩽m1\leqslant i\leqslant m, with the convenience that M0=1M_{0}=1. Then there exists a local factor chain (ℬ1′,…,ℬm′)(\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\prime},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\prime}) of resolution (M1′,…,Mm′)(M_{1}^{\prime},\dots,M_{m}^{\prime}) and modulus q′q^{\prime} such that (ℬ1′,…,ℬm′)(\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\prime},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\prime}) refines (ℬ1,…,ℬm)(\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}).

Proof.

First we prove the lemma in the special case q′=qq^{\prime}=q. For each 1⩽i⩽m1\leqslant i\leqslant m, we will apply Lemma 3.5 with ℬ=ℬi\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}_{i}, ℬ′′=ℬi−1\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime}=\mathcal{B}_{i-1} (taking ℬ0\mathcal{B}_{0} to be the trivial factor where each atom is a singleton), M=MiM=M_{i}, M′′=Mi−1M^{\prime\prime}=M_{i-1}, and M′=Mi′M^{\prime}=M_{i}^{\prime}. Hence we obtain a local factor ℬi′\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\prime} of resolution Mi′M_{i}^{\prime} and modulus qq, such that ℬi′\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\prime} refines ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} and ℬi−1\mathcal{B}_{i-1} refines ℬi′\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\prime}. The following diagram illustrates the construction in the case m=3m=3, where the dotted arrows represent refinement relations from applying Lemma 3.5:

Since ℬi−1′\mathcal{B}_{i-1}^{\prime} refines ℬi−1\mathcal{B}_{i-1} and ℬi−1\mathcal{B}_{i-1} refines ℬi′\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\prime}, it follows that ℬi−1′\mathcal{B}_{i-1}^{\prime} refines ℬi′\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\prime} for all 2⩽i⩽m2\leqslant i\leqslant m, as illustrated in the diagram above by the double arrows. Now we treat general q′q^{\prime}. By the above procedure, we first obtain a local factor chain (ℬ1′′,…,ℬm′′)(\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\prime\prime},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\prime\prime}) of resolution (q′​M1′/q,⋯,q′​Mm′/q)(q^{\prime}M_{1}^{\prime}/q,\cdots,q^{\prime}M_{m}^{\prime}/q) and modulus qq which refines (ℬ1,…,ℬm)(\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}). Next, for each 1⩽i⩽m1\leqslant i\leqslant m, divide each atom of ℬi′′\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\prime\prime} into residue classes modulo q′q^{\prime} to form a refinement ℬi′\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\prime} of ℬi′′\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\prime\prime}. This completes the proof. ∎

4. Polylogarithmic bound in the density result

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.1 using the improved density increment strategy developed by Heath-Brown [18] and Szemerédi [31]. For convenience, we follow the presentation in Green–Tao [15].

We begin by briefly outlining the idea. Assume that A⊆[N]A\subseteq[N] is a subset of density α\alpha that contains no nontrivial polynomial configurations. Since Lipschitz functions are nearly constant on long arithmetic progressions, Peluse [25] deduced from the inverse theorem (Theorem 2.4) and pigeonhole principle that that there exists a progression PP on which AA exhibits a density increment of size αO⁡(1)\alpha^{O(1)}. It turns out that this approach typically requires O⁡(α−O⁡(1))O(\alpha^{-O(1)}) iterations to reach a contradiction. The strategy adopted in this section improves on this by collecting several Lipschitz functions together to construct a new one, and then decomposing [N][N] into progressions on which this composite function is nearly constant. This refinement allows us to obtain a density increment of size c​αc\alpha on one of the progressions, thereby reducing the number of iterations to just O⁡(log⁡1/α)O(\log 1/\alpha). While the progressions used at each step are shorter than those in Peluse’s approach, it was observed in [15] that the progression length plays a less critical role in the overall argument.

Let us clarify the above argument. We first construct a nonnegative structural function g⩾0g\geqslant 0 such that it has the same mean value as 1A1_{A} (say, α\alpha), and the corresponding counting expressions weighted by gg and 1A1_{A} are comparable. This construction is formalized in Lemma 4.1 below. We then carry out the density-increment argument with respect to gg. Lemma 4.2, in essence, asserts that the density of gg increases by a factor of at least (1+c)​α(1+c)\alpha on some arithmetic progression.

5. Popular common difference

We plan to prove Theorem 1.2 in this section. The guiding philosophy of our approach aligns closely with that of [13, 28]. Specifically, given a function ff our goal is to find a regular function gg and a subset HH of [N][N] such that ff and gg exhibit similar densities of polynomial configurations with common differences in HH, while gg remains nearly constant under shifts by elements of HH.

To this end, we introduce the following expression in this section. Suppose that q⩽M⩽Nq\leqslant M\leqslant N are integers, and P1,…,Pm∈ℤ⁡[y]P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[y] are polynomials. Suppose that f0,…,fm:ℤ→ℂf_{0},\dots,f_{m}:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} are functions supported on the interval [N][N]. Set

ΛP1,…,PmN,M,q(f0,f1,…,fm)=N−1∑x∈ℤ𝔼y∈[M]q|yf0(x)f1(x+P1(y))⋯fm(x+Pm(y)).\Lambda^{N,M,q}_{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}}(f_{0},f_{1},\dots,f_{m})=N^{-1}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{y\in[M]\atop q|y}f_{0}(x)f_{1}(x+P_{1}(y))\cdots f_{m}(x+P_{m}(y)).

Given a function ff, the first step towards our goal is to find regular functions g1,…,gmg_{1},\dots,g_{m} and set H={y∈[M]:q|y}H=\left\{y\in[M]:q|y\right\} such that

ΛP1,…,PmN,M,q​(f,…,f)≈ΛP1,…,PmN,M,q​(f,g1,…,gm).\Lambda^{N,M,q}_{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}}(f,\dots,f)\approx\Lambda^{N,M,q}_{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}}(f,g_{1},\dots,g_{m}).

𝔼x∈Q(Πℬ1f)(x)⋯(Πℬm−1f)(x)⩾δQm−1.\mathbb{E}_{x\in Q}(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}f)(x)\cdots(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{m-1}}f)(x)\geqslant\delta_{Q}^{m-1}.

Since Πℬm​f\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{m}}f takes the value δP\delta_{P} on the atom P∈ℬmP\in\mathcal{B}_{m}, we have

𝔼x∈P(Πℬ1f)(x)⋯(Πℬmf)(x)=δP𝔼x∈P(Πℬ1f)(x)⋯(Πℬm−1f)(x).\mathbb{E}_{x\in P}(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}f)(x)\cdots(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{m}}f)(x)=\delta_{P}\mathbb{E}_{x\in P}(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}f)(x)\cdots(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{m-1}}f)(x).

Since ℬm−1\mathcal{B}_{m-1} refines ℬm\mathcal{B}_{m}, we may decompose PP as a disjoint union of atoms in ℬm−1\mathcal{B}_{m-1}, i.e. P=⊔Q∈ℬm−1∩PQP=\sqcup_{Q\in\mathcal{B}_{m-1}\cap P}Q, Using the inductive hypothesis and Hölder’s inequality, we get

𝔼x∈P(Πℬ1f)(x)⋯(Πℬm−1f)(x)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\in P}(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}f)(x)\cdots(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{m-1}}f)(x) =𝔼Q∈ℬm−1∩P𝔼x∈Q(Πℬ1f)(x)⋯(Πℬm−1f)(x)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{Q\in\mathcal{B}_{m-1}\cap P}\mathbb{E}_{x\in Q}(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}f)(x)\cdots(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{m-1}}f)(x)
⩾𝔼Q∈ℬm−1∩P​δQm−1⩾(𝔼Q∈ℬm−1∩P​𝔼x∈Q​f​(x))m−1⩾δPm−1.\displaystyle\geqslant\mathbb{E}_{Q\in\mathcal{B}_{m-1}\cap P}\delta_{Q}^{m-1}\geqslant(\mathbb{E}_{Q\in\mathcal{B}_{m-1}\cap P}\mathbb{E}_{x\in Q}f(x))^{m-1}\geqslant\delta_{P}^{m-1}.

Combining the above two inequalities, we conclude that

𝔼x∈P(Πℬ1f)(x)⋯(Πℬmf)(x)⩾δP⋅δPm−1=δPm,\mathbb{E}_{x\in P}(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}f)(x)\cdots(\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{m}}f)(x)\geqslant\delta_{P}\cdot\delta_{P}^{m-1}=\delta_{P}^{m},

as claimed.

∎
